meta.title: Who really said "God has no religion"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: "God has no religion" is pinned on Gandhi everywhere, but it appears in none of his writings. The line is actually Henry Whitney Bellows's, from an 1860 sermon — misattributed to Gandhi for decades.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'God has no religion'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Gandhi across the internet, but the exact phrase is in none of his works. It comes from Henry Whitney Bellows's 1860 Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine — a documented line misattributed to Gandhi.

answer.label: Not Gandhi — the line is Henry Whitney Bellows’s (1860)
answer.sourceLine: The three-word line circulates on hundreds of quote sites under Gandhi’s name, yet it appears in none of his writings — not the Collected Works, Young India, or Harijan — and it is absent even from Wikiquote’s Gandhi entry. The phrase is in fact a documented line from the American Unitarian minister Henry Whitney Bellows, who wrote “God has no religion” in his sermon “The Kingdom of God” (Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine, D. Appleton, 1860, p. 149) — decades before it was ever pinned on Gandhi.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: Henry W. Bellows, Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine (1860)
“All religions … proceed from the same God” (Young India, 29 May 1924)
Genuine Bellows line, misattributed to Gandhi

trail: The phrase does not appear anywhere on Wikiquote’s Gandhi page — not in its sourced, disputed, or misattributed sections.
On Goodreads and other aggregators the line is credited to Gandhi with no book, date, or citation attached.
Gandhi’s documented statements on the subject are different in wording — e.g. “all religions are more or less true … all proceed from the same God” (Young India, 29 May 1924).

The exact phrase is found in the published sermons of the Unitarian minister Henry Whitney Bellows: “… religion would have no occasion, and could have no existence. God has no religion. He worships no one; obeys no one” (Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine, sermon ‘The Kingdom of God’, 1860, p. 149).
source.excerptNote: Reproduced on quote sites under Gandhi’s name with no date, work, or page — but the wording is traceable: it comes from Bellows’s 1860 sermon ‘The Kingdom of God’, where it means that religion is a human relation to God, not an attribute of God himself.

Gandhi’s genuine parallel statements from the 1920s–30s are separately under the stewardship of the Navajivan Trust / Gandhi Heritage Portal.

author.name: Henry Whitney Bellows
author.heading: About Henry Whitney Bellows
author.bio: Henry Whitney Bellows (1814–1882) was an American Unitarian clergyman and author. The line “God has no religion” appears in his 1860 book Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine, in the sermon “The Kingdom of God” (p. 149) — long before it was ever credited to Mahatma Gandhi, whose own documented view was a religious pluralism that all faiths are imperfect human roads to the same God.

cite.sourceCitation: Henry W. Bellows, “The Kingdom of God,” in Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine, in Twenty-Five Sermons (New York: D. Appleton, 1860), p. 149. The exact line reads “God has no religion. He worships no one; obeys no one.” Long misattributed to Gandhi, whose nearest genuine statement is “all religions … proceed from the same God” (Young India, 29 May 1924).

misattribution.heading: The real author isn’t Gandhi — it’s Bellows
misattribution.intro: The line is one of the internet’s most-shared “Gandhi” quotes, but the trail doesn’t end at the aggregator sites: the exact wording was published decades earlier by the American Unitarian minister Henry Whitney Bellows.

items.why: Repeated across Goodreads, AZQuotes, and QuoteFancy with no work, date, or page — and absent from Wikiquote and from his Collected Works.

The exact phrase appears verbatim in the Unitarian minister’s Re-Statements of Christian Doctrine (D. Appleton, 1860): “… religion would have no occasion, and could have no existence. God has no religion. He worships no one; obeys no one” — from the sermon ‘The Kingdom of God’ (p. 149). Goodreads even tags the line ‘misattributed-to-gandhi’.

misattribution.truthLine: What Gandhi actually taught was that faiths are “different roads converging to the same point” and that all religions “proceed from the same God” (Young India, 29 May 1924) — a kindred sentiment, but not the source of this three-word line, which is Bellows’s.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Gandhi
lead: The sentiment fits Gandhi so well that few readers pause to source it. His life’s work argued that no single creed monopolizes the divine — a message that compresses neatly into “God has no religion.” That very fit is what lets a line Gandhi never wrote pass as one of his.

But fit is not evidence. Under Gandhi’s name the phrase surfaces only on modern quote sites with no date or work — while its true home is an 1860 sermon by Henry Whitney Bellows, and Gandhi’s own formulations of the kindred idea are longer, dated, and printed in Young India and Hind Swaraj.
context.pull: The idea is Gandhi’s; the exact words are Henry Whitney Bellows’s.
